regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 54.6","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY flatters. IIP overall slowed to 6.7% YoY from 8.8%, and core sector decelerated to 5.4% YoY from 6.0% — the goods economy is losing altitude even as PMI composite at 54.6 holds up on services. The quality question: capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is healthy, but if the credit surge funding industry (20% YoY) is pulling forward demand rather than building genuine productive capacity, the IIP print six months from now will be the tell.","badge_label":"Slowing Pace","badge_type":"b-slow"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 4.45% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 4.45% YoY understates the pressure building in the pipeline. Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY — a 95th-percentile print — feeds into WPI at 9.92% YoY with a 2-3 quarter lag into core goods prices. Core CPI at 3.9% YoY looks contained today; the inversion is that RBI's own revised inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY implies they expect core to move — which makes any near-term rate cut a credibility risk, not a policy option.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 17.1% YoY; CD ratio 81.4%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 17.1% YoY against deposit growth of 10.8% YoY is a 630 bps divergence that the CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits — 75th percentile historically — only partially captures. The second-order effect runs through NBFCs: credit to NBFCs accelerating to 14.9% YoY from 10.6% signals they are plugging their own deposit gap with wholesale bank funding. The last time CD ratios sustained above 80% in a rising-rate global environment, macro-prudential tightening via risk weights followed within two quarters.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is on hold, but the real rate is being compressed from both sides — CPI rising, RBI stationary. With RBI's own inflation forecast now at 5.1% YoY, the real repo rate is barely positive. The INR at 97.09 adds a third constraint: cutting rates while the currency depreciates and fuel inflation runs at 22.93% YoY would import inflation faster than domestic easing could stimulate. The RBI is not driving — it is being driven.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.1% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — up from 75.6% — is the most credible signal of a genuine investment upcycle. At 74th percentile, utilisation is high enough to justify new capacity without triggering overcapacity risk. The one soft spot is core sector at 5.4% YoY, down from 6.0%, but infrastructure output typically lags capital goods orders by 4-6 quarters. Industry credit surging to 20% YoY from 6.5% confirms the capex signal is not a statistical artefact.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹199853 cr/mo; PV 16% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹1,99,853 cr / month is a strong print, but the composition matters: passenger vehicle sales at 16% YoY and two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY suggest both urban and rural demand are participating. Two-wheeler strength is the informal economy's vital sign — it does not lie. The tension is that credit card growth has collapsed to 2.3% YoY from 5.6%, suggesting urban discretionary spending is being funded less by revolving credit and more by income — which is structurally healthier but implies the consumption ceiling is lower than the GST headline suggests.","badge_label":"Demand Surge","badge_type":"b-exp"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 17.1% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 10.8% YoY creates a 630 bps divergence. CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (down from 82.5% prior month) remains elevated at 75th percentile historically. Credit-to-deposit gap has widened for 3 consecutive months: 82.5% → 81.4%. NBFC credit growth accelerating at 14.9% YoY (up from 10.6% YoY prior) signals wholesale funding pressure. Industry credit surging at 20% YoY and services credit at 22.9% YoY — both concentrated in sectors with higher wholesale dependency.","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% and deposit franchises in metros (HDFC Bank, Kotak, ICICI). Underweight NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities and those dependent on CP/bond markets. RBI will likely signal deposit-friendly measures (higher savings rate ceilings, CRR cuts) within 2-3 months if divergence persists. Avoid small finance banks with <30% CASA.","pct_10y":75,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 75th percentile is historically tight. Prior episodes at this level (2018, 2021) preceded either RBI liquidity injections or credit slowdowns. Current divergence is the widest in 18 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Cycle Firing on All Cylinders","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY (latest) signals robust investment demand. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6% prior month) — at 74th percentile, indicating headroom for capex without overcapacity risk. Core sector growth at 5.4% YoY (down from 6% prior) is the only soft spot, but this lags capex by 1-2 quarters. Credit to industry surging at 20% YoY (up from 6.5% YoY prior) and credit to agriculture at 17% YoY (up from 7.3% YoY) show broad-based investment appetite. Vehicle credit at 18.8% YoY and personal credit at 16.2% YoY confirm consumption-led capex multiplier.","implication":"Overweight capital goods manufacturers (Cummins, Timken, Rane Brake), cement (Ambuja, ACC), and steel (Tata Steel, JSW Steel). Capex cycle typically runs 18-24 months; we are in month 8-10. Avoid defensive plays; rotate into cyclicals. Infrastructure contractors (L&T, Godrej & Boyce) will see order inflows accelerate in Q4 FY26. Expect IIP capgoods to sustain 12-15% through FY26.","pct_10y":52,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle; historically, capex accelerates when CU crosses 75%. This level preceded the 2014-2016 capex boom and the 2021-2023 recovery.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"Affluent Money Entering Via SIP Backdoor","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,297 cr / month (up from ₹31,961 cr / month prior, rising 2 in a row). SIP AUM at ₹18.62 lakh cr (up from ₹18.21 lakh cr, rising 2 in a row) — at 93rd percentile. SIP accounts at 100.18 mn (up from 99.06 mn) — at 82nd percentile. MF AUM at ₹87.08 lakh cr (rising 2 in a row) and average AUM at ₹88.31 lakh cr (at 88th percentile). Equity MF net inflows at ₹29,329 cr / month (up from ₹24,697 cr / month). DII equity net at ₹58,502 cr / month (at 100th percentile, rising 2 in a row) — domestic institutions are the marginal buyer.","implication":"SIP AUM growing 2.3% MoM while SIP accounts growing 1.1% MoM implies average ticket size rising — affluent retail entering via systematic route, not mass retail. This is late-cycle behaviour. Overweight large-cap quality (Nifty 50 constituents with ROE > 18%) and avoid micro-cap/small-cap momentum plays. Expect SIP inflows to sustain but growth rate to decelerate as base effects kick in. Domestic flows are offsetting FII weakness (FII net at ₹29,631 cr / month, volatile).","pct_10y":92,"pct_note":"SIP AUM at 93rd percentile is near all-time highs. Prior peaks (2021, 2023) preceded 15-20% market corrections. Current inflow momentum is strong but valuation-dependent.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI Credibility","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (up from 20.05% YoY prior month) — at 95th percentile, the highest in 18 months. WPI at 9.92% YoY (up from 9.78% YoY) signals broad-based input cost pressure. Brent crude at $103.81/bbl (flat from $103.81/bbl prior) but trending up from $100.5/bbl 2 months ago. Natural gas at $3.134/MMBtu (up from $3.04/MMBtu 3 months ago). CPI headline at 4.45% YoY (up from 4.38% YoY) and RBI's inflation forecast revised up to 5.1% YoY (from 4.6% YoY prior). Food inflation at 5.52% YoY (up from 5.32% YoY) adds to headline pressure.","implication":"RBI's 4% target is now at risk; inflation trajectory points to 5.0-5.2% by Q2 FY26. This constrains rate cuts to H2 FY26 at earliest. Overweight energy stocks (ONGC, Reliance) and underweight rate-sensitive sectors (NBFCs, auto finance). Hedge INR weakness via commodity longs (Brent, natural gas). India's oil import bill will rise ₹2,000-3,000 cr / month if Brent stays above $100/bbl, pressuring CAD. Avoid long-duration bonds; 10Y Treasury at 5.28% yield (96th percentile) is a headwind.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a structural risk. Prior episodes (2021-2022, 2011-2012) preceded either RBI tightening or currency depreciation. Current spike is driven by geopolitical risk and OPEC+ production cuts.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"Fed Tightening Bias Resurfaces; Carry Unwind Risk","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63% p.a., rising 2 in a row) — at 68th percentile. US 10Y Treasury yield at 5.28% (at 96th percentile, up from 5.27% prior) — highest in 18 months. US CPI at 3.353% YoY (up from 3.304% YoY, rising 2 in a row) and US core PCE at 3.008% YoY (up from 2.984% YoY). BOJ rate at 1.0% p.a. (up from 0.75% p.a., at 86th percentile) — policy divergence widening. ECB deposit rate at 2.25% p.a. (up from 2.0% p.a.). US PMI composite at 56 index (at 84th percentile, up from 54.5 index) signals US growth resilience. DXY at 102.064 index (flat, at 55th percentile) but trending up from 101.9 index.","implication":"Carry trade unwind risk is rising. INR weakness (97.09 ₹/USD, at 94th percentile, up 4 of last 5 months) is a direct consequence of Fed tightening bias and BOJ tightening. Overweight USD-denominated assets and underweight INR-denominated bonds. Expect 10Y Indian government securities to trade 50-75 bps wider vs US Treasuries. FII equity flows will remain volatile; current ₹29,631 cr / month is unsustainable if US rates stay elevated. Hedge via long USD positions or short INR forwards.","pct_10y":96,"pct_note":"US 10Y Treasury at 96th percentile is a structural headwind for EM carry trades. Prior episodes (2018, 2022) saw sharp EM currency depreciation and equity outflows. Current divergence (Fed tightening, BOJ tightening, ECB steady) is the widest in 3 years.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Depreciation Accelerates; RBI Intervention Likely","data_text":"INR at 97.09 ₹/USD (up from 96.78 ₹/USD prior, rising 4 of last 5 months) — at 94th percentile. Recent trend: 96.15 → 95.24 → 96.15 → 97.09 shows accelerating weakness. India VIX at 15.275 index (up from 13.89 index, at 10th percentile) — volatility is low, suggesting orderly depreciation rather than panic. FII equity net at ₹29,631 cr / month (up from ₹20,200 cr / month prior, but volatile: -114 → -3,111.9 → 29,631) — flows are inconsistent. Gold in INR at ₹13,033/g (up from ₹12,992/g, at 100th percentile) — INR weakness is broad-based. Brent at $103.81/bbl and natural gas at $3.134/MMBtu add to import pressure.","implication":"RBI will likely intervene to defend 97.50 ₹/USD level; expect RBI to sell USD reserves or hike CRR to absorb liquidity. INR weakness will persist if Fed stays hawkish and oil stays elevated. Overweight INR hedges (long USD forwards, short INR puts). Avoid INR-denominated long-duration bonds; 10Y yields at 6.5-6.7% are insufficient compensation for depreciation risk. Exporters (IT, pharma, textiles) will see margin expansion; importers (oil, electronics) will face headwinds. CAD will widen to 1.5-2.0% of GDP if INR stays weak.","pct_10y":94,"pct_note":"INR at 94th percentile weakness is the highest in 18 months. Prior episodes (2022, 2018) saw INR depreciate 8-12% before RBI intervention stabilised the currency. Current trajectory suggests 98-99 ₹/USD is possible if Fed stays hawkish.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Shift, Not IT Weakness","data_text":"Office absorption at 13.2 mn sq ft / quarter (down from 13.7 mn sq ft / quarter, at 6th percentile) — lowest in 18 months. Office vacancy at 14.5% vacant (down from 14.7% vacant, at 42nd percentile). Yet Nifty IT is flat (Nifty 50 down 1.7% MoM) and IT credit growth at 22.9% YoY (services credit, at 76th percentile). Rent in Bengaluru at ₹163/sqft/mo (up from ₹148/sqft/mo, at 95th percentile, rising 2 of last 5 quarters) and rent in Mumbai at ₹335/sqft/mo (at 100th percentile, rising 2 of last 5 quarters). Retail mall vacancy at 5% vacant (down from 7.5% vacant, at 8th percentile) — retail is absorbing space faster than offices. RE launches at 114.32 units / quarter (up from 106 units / quarter) and RE sales at 100.22 units / quarter (up from 90.715 units / quarter) — residential is booming. Unsold inventory at 630,590 units (up from 616,000 units, at 65th percentile) — but this is residential, not office.","implication":"Office absorption collapse is NOT an IT services weakness signal — it reflects GCC (Global Capability Centres) consolidation into fewer, larger campuses and hybrid work adoption. Traditional IT services (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) are shedding leased space; GCCs (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Apple) are consolidating into premium Grade-A buildings. Rent inflation in Bengaluru and Mumbai is driven by GCC demand, not IT services. Overweight Grade-A office REITs (Embassy, Mindspace) in Bengaluru and Mumbai — they will capture GCC consolidation. Underweight mid-tier office parks and IT parks. Residential RE is the real story: affordability at 3.5x price ÷ income (up from 0.38x prior, at 19th percentile) signals affordability stress, yet sales are rising — this is affluent money, not mass retail. Expect residential launches to moderate in H2 FY26 as affordability constraints bite.","pct_10y":6,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 6th percentile is a structural shift, not cyclical weakness. Prior low absorption periods (2020, 2015) preceded either IT services consolidation or economic slowdowns. Current episode is GCC-driven consolidation — a positive for premium office and a negative for mid-tier IT parks.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, 6.7% IIP — Services Papering Over a Goods Slowdown

The facts:

  • PMI Composite at 54.6 (83rd percentile) holds up — but manufacturing PMI slipped to 52.8 from 53.5 while services PMI rose to 54.5 from 53.3: the divergence is widening.
  • IIP YoY slowed to 6.7% YoY from 8.8%; core sector decelerated to 5.4% YoY from 6.0% — goods output losing momentum even as capital goods at 16.1% YoY signals investment intent.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY and PV sales at 16% YoY confirm rural and urban consumption are both alive — GST at ₹1,99,853 cr / month corroborates.
  • But capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile) is the ceiling: private capex will not accelerate meaningfully until this crosses 80%.

The tension: GDP at 7.8% YoY is a services-led number; the goods economy — IIP, core sector, manufacturing PMI — is decelerating in parallel. The headline is not wrong, but it is incomplete.

Bottom line: Watch manufacturing PMI: a print below 52 would confirm the goods-services split is widening into a structural drag, not a seasonal dip.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Resilience Exports Tightening — India Pays the INR Tax

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 56 (84th percentile) and US GDP SAAR at 2.2% SAAR — rising from 1.5% — give the Fed no reason to pivot; Fed Funds at 3.75% p.a. rose for the second consecutive month.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.28% yield (96th percentile) is doing the tightening the Fed hasn't — real economy stress is embedded in the curve, not the policy rate.
  • China GDP at 4.3% YoY (down from 5.0%) with PMI Composite at 49.5 (contraction) removes the commodity reflation backstop India's CAD needs.
  • But Euro Stoxx 50 at 6,127 (100th percentile) is still pricing a soft landing that the bond market — and China's PMI — are not confirming.

The tension: US growth resilience keeps the Fed on hold and 10Y yields elevated; China's deceleration prevents commodity prices from easing. India sits at the intersection of both pressures — import bill rising, carry attractiveness falling.

Bottom line: If US 10Y sustains above 5.30% yield, INR pressure intensifies and RBI's FX reserve deployment accelerates — watch the weekly reserve print.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

Domestic Flows at Record Highs — But Funding the Wrong Side of the Trade

The facts:

  • DII equity net at ₹58,502 cr / month (100th percentile, rising two in a row) — domestic institutions are the marginal buyer as FII flows remain volatile: ₹29,631 cr / month this month after two months of net selling.
  • SIP inflows at ₹32,297 cr / month (92nd percentile) and SIP AUM at ₹18.62 lakh cr (93rd percentile) — retail participation is structurally deepening.
  • But bank deposit growth at 10.8% YoY vs credit growth at 17.1% YoY means the same household saving that funds SIPs is not flowing into bank deposits — the system's funding base is thinning.
  • NBFC credit growth accelerating to 14.9% YoY from 10.6% signals wholesale funding demand is rising precisely as the deposit pool tightens.

The tension: Equity liquidity is abundant — SIPs and DIIs are at record levels. Banking system liquidity is structurally stressed — the CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits reflects a savings allocation shift that equity markets are celebrating and credit markets should fear.

Bottom line: Avoid leveraged NBFC exposure; the wholesale funding squeeze will show in Q3 NIM prints before it shows in NPAs.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

NRI Demand and Domestic SIPs Hold the Floor — REITs Signal the Ceiling

The facts:

  • NRI residential buying is RISING — NRI share at 20% of purchases (up from 15%, +5 pp), with 25% share within premium/luxury; INR at 97.09 makes dollar-denominated buyers 3% cheaper than six months ago.
  • Hyderabad leads city momentum: sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY, but 29 months of unsold inventory is a supply overhang that price momentum cannot sustain indefinitely.
  • Office REITs tell a different story — Embassy at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — all down sharply from prior levels as office absorption at 13.2 mn sq ft / quarter (6th percentile) disappoints.
  • But Nifty 50 at 22,232 (72nd percentile) with Bank Nifty at 54,515 (89th percentile) — equity valuations have not yet repriced the NIM compression that the CD ratio implies.

The tension: Residential real estate is supported by NRI flows and INR weakness; office REITs are being repriced lower as absorption data contradicts rent levels. Equities are pricing capex optimism while ignoring banking system funding stress.

Bottom line: Overweight residential developers with NRI-facing premium inventory in Mumbai and Bengaluru; underweight office REITs until absorption recovers above 16 mn sq ft / quarter.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Detonator — INR Is the Common Thread

The facts:

  • INR at 97.09 (94th percentile, weakening 4 of last 5 months) — Brent at $103.81/bbl means every further 2% INR depreciation adds ~₹8,000 cr / month to the import bill.
  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) — if Brent crosses $110/bbl, RBI's revised forecast of 5.1% YoY CPI becomes a floor, not a ceiling, eliminating any rate-cut optionality.
  • CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (75th percentile) with NBFC credit at 14.9% YoY — a macro-prudential risk-weight circular on unsecured or NBFC lending would reprice ₹15–20 lakh cr of credit overnight.
  • US 10Y at 5.28% yield (96th percentile) — a sustained move above 5.40% would trigger EM carry unwind; India's $680 bn FX reserves buffer is large but not infinite against coordinated outflows.

The tension: Each risk is individually manageable; the danger is sequencing — INR weakness feeds fuel inflation, which locks out rate cuts, which keeps real rates low, which accelerates deposit-to-equity migration, which tightens bank funding further.

Bottom line: Watch Friday's RBI weekly FX reserve data: a drawdown exceeding $3 bn in a single week signals active INR defence and raises the probability of emergency macro-prudential action.

"}
